summary:
FLIRA (Flame in Freefall) is an SI powered fire safety intelligence platform designed to support safer human space exploration. It transforms NASA's extensive microgravity combustion research into accessible, interactive, and actionable insights for future spacecraft, lunar habitats, and Martian missions.
The platform integrates NASA PSI datasets, intelligent investigation ranking, scientific visualization, computational physics modelling, and an AI powered research copilot. Users can discover and compare combustion experiments, evaluate their relevance to mission specific conditions such as gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, and airflow, and explore flame behaviour through an interactive virtual laboratory.
FLIRA also provides evidence linked AI assistance using hybrid information retrieval and knowledge graphs technique helping users understand complex research findings. Its uncertainty aware modelling highlights important knowledge gaps, particularly the lack of experimental partial-gravity combustion data.
By connecting decades of NASA research with future mission requirements, FLIRA aims to help researchers identify fire hazards, improve safety strategies, and make human exploration of the Moon and Mars safer.
details:
FLIRA — Flame in Freefall

FLIRA (Flame in Freefall) is an AI powered fire-safety intelligence platform designed to make human space exploration safer. It transforms NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity combustion research into accessible, interactive insights that can support fire safety planning for spacecraft, lunar habitats, and future Mars missions.

What does the project do, and how does it work?

FLIRA brings NASA combustion investigations and experimental data together in one interactive dashboard. Its investigation ranking system helps users identify research relevant to mission conditions, considering factors such as gravity, oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, airflow, and fuel material.

The platform includes an interactive virtual laboratory where users can adjust environmental parameters and explore model based flame behaviour. It also provides investigation comparisons, scientific visualizations, a research knowledge base, and an AI powered copilot that helps users explore research findings with supporting source references.

What benefits does it provide?

  • Makes complex NASA combustion research easier to discover, understand, and compare.
  • Helps researchers identify experiments relevant to specific spacecraft and habitat conditions.
  • Provides an interactive way to explore how environmental parameters may influence flame behaviour.
  • Connects research findings with historical spaceflight fire incidents and safety lessons.
  • Highlights research gaps, especially the shortage of experimental combustion data under actual lunar and Martian partial-gravity conditions.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to support better informed fire-prevention, detection, and suppression research for future human space missions. By making existing evidence more accessible and highlighting unanswered scientific questions, FLIRA can help researchers and mission planners identify relevant studies and areas where further experiments are needed. It is a research support tool, not a certified spacecraft fire safety system.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using React 18, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS. Python scripts support data preparation and ingestion. We used NASA PSI datasets, JSON and CSV knowledge resources, Lucide React icons, and Vitest for testing. The AI copilot can connect to Google Gemini and OpenRouter, with a local retrieval based fallback. The application is designed as a web platform and does not require specialized hardware.

How is the project creative?

FLIRA combines scientific data exploration, mission-specific investigation ranking, interactive physics based modelling, visual analytics, and AI assisted research in one platform. Instead of presenting NASA research as disconnected documents and tables, it creates an interactive environment where users can explore relationships between experiments and future mission conditions.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered gravity differences between Earth, the Moon, Mars, and microgravity, oxygen concentration, cabin pressure , ventilation and airflow, fuel type and material, experimental evidence, uncertainty in model based estimates, historical spacecraft fire incidents, and the practical needs of future crews and researchers. We also considered the importance of distinguishing measured experimental results from model-generated estimates.
